title: The first community (Acts 2:42–47)
hookLine: teaching, breaking bread, prayers, and all things in common
carry: they held all things in common

cards: Anyone have a ladder? A cup of sugar? A ride to the airport on Thursday?

The group chat for a building or a street runs on questions like that, and usually somebody answers. Now take it all the way. Luke says that after Pentecost about three thousand people were baptized in a single day.
A small group from Galilee became a crowd. So what did they do next? Luke answers in one short paragraph, six verses long.

teach.b: Here's the heart of it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." In Luke's Greek, that's four things.
The apostles' teaching: they kept learning.

teach.h: KOINONIA: HAVING A PART IN EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Fellowship, the Greek word koinonia: sharing, having a part in each other. The breaking of bread: meals together, and, as Catholics read it, the Eucharist.
And the prayers, including, Luke says, going up to the temple every day. They were Jews, and they kept praying where they always had.
Then this: "And all they that believed, were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and handed out the money to anyone in need.
They ate with glad and simple hearts, Luke says, and people liked them. Now, the honest reading. This wasn't a system anyone was forced into.
A few chapters later Peter tells a man that his land was his own to keep. Giving was free. Not every church since has lived exactly like this.
Catholic religious life draws on it: monks and nuns vow to hold their goods in common.
And the Church teaches something for everyone: the goods of the earth are meant, in the end, for all people, so what you own is also held for others. Four pillars, and one open hand.

how: Catholic religious communities hold their goods in common, and parishes gather around the same four things: teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist and prayer, with collections and ministries for people in need.

games.why: they sold possessions and handed the money out as anyone had need, freely. and they ate together with glad and simple hearts.

practice: Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, and find one thing that sits unused while someone else could use it: a coat, a tool, a book, a spare hour on Saturday.
Don't pick the thing that's easiest to get rid of; pick the one that would actually help someone, and hold it in your mind. If you pray, you can ask who it's meant for.

wordCard.voice: koinonia. The Greek word for fellowship, for sharing a part in each other's lives, one mark of the first believers.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, having a part in something together. one of the four marks of the first community.
